reference.source: Renal tubulopathy and clinical genetics references
clinicalPearls: Caused by loss-of-function of the apical inwardly-rectifying potassium channel ROMK (Kir1.1), encoded by KCNJ1, which recycles potassium to sustain NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb.
Another antenatal (neonatal) Bartter subtype with severe polyhydramnios and premature birth.
Distinctive transient neonatal hyperkalaemia occurs before the expected hypokalaemia emerges, because ROMK also mediates potassium secretion in the collecting duct.
Once established, the biochemistry converges on hypokalaemic hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis with hyperreninaemic hyperaldosteronism and normal or low blood pressure.
Hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis are prominent, as in type 1.
Prostaglandin E2 is elevated, and prostaglandin synthetase inhibition ameliorates the salt wasting and polyuria.
Salt craving, polyuria, recurrent dehydration and failure to thrive dominate the neonatal picture.
The early hyperkalaemic phase can be mistaken for pseudohypoaldosteronism or adrenal insufficiency.
reference.pathophysiology: Bartter syndrome type 2 is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in KCNJ1, which encodes the apical inwardly-rectifying potassium channel ROMK (Kir1.1) of the thick ascending limb. ROMK recycles potassium back into the tubular lumen to sustain the activity of the NKCC2 cotransporter; without adequate luminal potassium, sodium chloride reabsorption in the loop fails and the biochemical picture ultimately converges on that of type 1, with salt wasting, secondary hyperaldosteronism, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis. Because ROMK also mediates potassium secretion in the cortical collecting duct, affected neonates characteristically pass through a transient period of hyperkalaemia before chronic renal potassium wasting supervenes and hypokalaemia becomes established. As in the other antenatal forms, overproduction of prostaglandin E2 amplifies renin release, contributing to polyuria and progressive volume depletion, and its inhibition is therapeutically beneficial.
additionalDifferentials: Bartter syndrome type 1 (SLC12A1 / NKCC2) — antenatal, without the transient hyperkalaemic phase
Bartter syndrome type 3 (CLCNKB / ClC-Kb) — classic, later onset with a broader phenotype
Bartter syndrome type 4 (BSND / barttin) — antenatal salt wasting with sensorineural deafness
Transient antenatal Bartter syndrome type 5 (MAGED2, X-linked)
Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 — a key mimic during the early transient hyperkalaemic phase
Gitelman syndrome (SLC12A3) — hypocalciuric, hypomagnesaemic, later onset
Primary adrenal insufficiency presenting with neonatal hyperkalaemia and salt wasting
additionalInvestigations: Serial serum electrolytes and venous blood gas, tracking the early transient hyperkalaemia and the later switch to hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis
Plasma renin activity and aldosterone, both characteristically elevated
Renal tract ultrasound looking for nephrocalcinosis
Serum magnesium, usually preserved, to help distinguish from Gitelman syndrome
Molecular genetic testing of KCNJ1 within an inherited tubulopathy gene panel
redFlags: Dangerous neonatal hyperkalaemia during the early transient phase, with electrocardiographic changes
Subsequent severe hypokalaemia with cardiac arrhythmia
Profound salt-wasting dehydration and circulatory collapse
Complications of extreme prematurity following polyhydramnios
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally favourable once the neonatal period, including the transient hyperkalaemic phase, is navigated and replacement therapy with prostaglandin synthetase inhibition is established. Nephrocalcinosis and some long-term reduction in renal function may nonetheless develop.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting the early transient hyperkalaemia as pseudohypoaldosteronism or adrenal insufficiency and delaying the correct diagnosis
Assuming potassium will remain stable and missing the later transition to hypokalaemia
Confusing the established biochemistry with Gitelman syndrome
